opus-5.5.text:
I actually feel pretty optimistic about it, though I understand why a lot of mathematicians feel a mix of excitement and anxiety.

The way I think about it is that mathematics has never really been about the mechanical act of grinding out a proof. Proofs are how we certify that something is true, but the deeper reason people do math is to understand. Why is this structure here? Why do these two seemingly unrelated areas talk to each other? If AI can take over more and more of the verification, the case-checking, even finding proofs of conjectures we pose, then I think humans get pushed toward the most interesting parts: asking the right questions, building new frameworks, deciding what is worth knowing.

There's a historical parallel I like. When computers started doing massive calculations, people worried that it would hollow out certain kinds of mathematical work. Instead it opened up whole new fields, and things like the four color theorem or computer-assisted proofs became part of the landscape. I think AI for math, especially when it's combined with formal verification in languages like Lean, could be a much bigger version of that. You get a system that doesn't just say "here's an answer," but "here's an answer and a machine-checked guarantee that it's correct." That changes how much we can trust, and how fast we can build on each other's work.

Will it feel strange if one day an AI proves a famous open problem? Absolutely. There will be a bit of an identity question for our community. But I'd rather frame it as: we're building a collaborator that can explore the mathematical universe much faster than we can, and our job becomes being the explorers who decide where to point the telescope, and then making sense of what we see. Understanding is still a human experience. A proof existing somewhere in a database doesn't automatically mean humanity understands it, and translating machine discoveries into human insight is going to be a huge and beautiful area of work.

So, honestly, I see it less as AI replacing mathematicians and more as mathematics finally getting to scale. And for someone like me who fell in love with math as a kid, the idea that we might discover far more of it in our lifetimes is incredibly exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says AI will act as a collaborator and humans will still interpret discoveries, but it does not clearly state that mathematics’ communal culture will persist.

r002.rationale: It describes humans as explorers who choose where to direct AI and says discovering much more mathematics is exciting, conveying continued enjoyment of creative exploration alongside faster AI proof work.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't find that future scary. I find it exciting, and I also think the question hides an assumption I'd push back on.

When people say "everything mathematicians can do," they usually mean proving theorems. And yes, I think AI will get very good at that, probably faster than most people in the community expected two years ago. We've already seen models go from struggling with competition problems to producing gold-medal-level solutions, and the gap between that and research-level proof is narrowing. If you'd asked me as a student at MIT whether a machine would ever write a proof I couldn't find, I would have said maybe in my lifetime. Now I think it's a question of years.

But mathematics is not only proof-finding. It's deciding what's worth proving. It's taste. It's noticing that two fields that look unrelated are secretly the same structure. Most of the great mathematicians I admire are remembered not for the hardest theorem they proved but for the questions they asked that opened a door for everyone else. I'm much less sure that part gets automated on the same timeline, and even if it does, I think humans will still want to be in that room.

The other thing I'd say is that the fear usually comes from a scarcity mindset, the idea that there's a fixed amount of mathematics and if the machine does it, there's nothing left for us. That's just not how the field works. Every tool that made mathematics easier, from symbolic algebra to computer-assisted proof, ended up expanding what people could ask. There are thousands of open problems where the bottleneck is simply that no human has enough hours to try. If AI can do the grinding, mathematicians get to spend their time on the parts that actually require a human point of view.

So the honest answer is that I'm building toward that future on purpose. At Axiom, our whole premise is that you want a system that can both reason informally like a mathematician and verify formally so that you can trust the output. If that works, the role of the mathematician doesn't disappear. It changes. You become more like a conductor and less like someone playing every instrument yourself.

And personally, if a machine solves a problem I've been stuck on for years, my first reaction will be to read the proof. That's the part I'm in it for.

r001.rationale: The response says humans will still want to help choose questions and that mathematicians’ roles will change, but it does not clearly state that mathematics’ communal culture will persist.

r002.rationale: The response welcomes AI’s ability to handle proof work and says the speaker would eagerly read a solution to a problem they had struggled with, showing continued interest in mathematical exploration.

astra-6.text:
I think I’d feel both excited and a little unsettled. If AI could do everything mathematicians can do, we might get answers to questions that have been out of reach for a very long time. But part of the joy of mathematics is working through something you don’t understand and finally seeing why it’s true. Having an answer available doesn’t necessarily replace that experience.

For me, a lot would depend on whether these systems could help us understand their discoveries. There’s a difference between being told that a conjecture is true and gaining a new way to think about it. I’d be excited about a future where AI expands what we can understand, even if that changes what being a mathematician looks like.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the joy of understanding mathematics and how AI may change mathematicians’ work, but it does not state that mathematics’ human communal culture will persist.

r002.rationale: It says part of mathematics’ joy is working through something not understood and finally seeing why it is true, and suggests AI answers would not replace that experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’d feel both excited and a little unsettled. There’s the possibility of understanding things we’ve struggled with for a very long time, and that’s wonderful. But if you love doing mathematics, you also love the process—the confusion, trying an idea, finally seeing why something works. Having an AI that can give you an answer doesn’t necessarily take away the value of going through that yourself.

I’d also distinguish between AI being able to do everything mathematicians can do and humans having nothing left to contribute. We might spend more time deciding which questions we care about, or trying to understand the ideas behind a proof. And even if AI could do those things too, I think I’d still want to do mathematics. Understanding something for yourself is a different experience from knowing that someone—or something—else understands it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses individual enjoyment and human contributions, but does not say that the communal culture of mathematics will persist.

r002.rationale: The response says people who love mathematics will still value the process of trying ideas and understanding why something works, even if AI can provide answers.
